item.title: [40%] [bioRxiv Neuroscience] Compositional computations in the primate frontal cortex
item.description:
Relevance: 40% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience

A hallmark of intelligence is the ability to apply familiar operations to new inputs without relearning. How neural circuits carry a learned computation into states never visited during training remains unclear. Here we combined neural recordings, circuit modeling and human experiments to investigate compositional generalization. Monkeys learned to combine a start location with a displacement specified by the direction and duration of an optic-flow stimulus, then encountered novel combinations of these familiar inputs. Frontal population activity separated the computation into spatial and temporal components: start location and flow direction established the neural state, from which activity evolved along shared timing dynamics. Novel combinations elicited accurate responses when trajectories maintained this organization, whereas departures predicted systematic behavioral biases. Circuit models revealed a three-way alignment problem: input representations, recurrent dynamics and readout operations must jointly implement the required computation. Mismatches produced systematic biases that increased with distance from trained conditions. Humans exhibited similar biases when familiar sensory cues and spatial transformations were linked through an unfamiliar mapping. Together, these findings show how the coordination of reusable neural resources supports new computations, and how its disruption produces predictable failures of generalization.

item.title: [35%] [arXiv Neurons and Cognition] A multi-scale information geometry reveals the structure of mutual information in neural populations
item.description:
Relevance: 35% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition

arXiv:2605.06304v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding how neural population responses represent sensory information is a central problem in systems neuroscience. One approach is to define a representational geometry on stimulus space in which distances reflect how reliably stimuli can be distinguished from neural activity. However, different constructions of these distances can lead to qualitatively different conclusions about the neural code. Here, we show that a unique Riemannian representational geometry emerges from first principles governing how distances contract as stimulus resolution is lost through coarse-graining. This results in a multi-scale extension of the Fisher information metric, capturing encoding structure from fine stimulus details to coarse global distinctions. The resulting geometry is exactly related to the mutual information encoded by the population: well-encoded stimulus directions (those contributing more to mutual information) are expanded, whereas poorly encoded directions are contracted. The metric tensor can be estimated using diffusion models, making the framework practical for large neural populations and high-dimensional stimuli. Applied to visual cortical responses to natural images, the eigenvectors of the metric tensor identify stimulus variations that contribute most to the encoded stimulus information, yielding interpretable features that are robust to modelling choices. Together, these results provide a principled, information-theoretic framework for characterising neural population codes.

item.title: [34%] [bioRxiv Neuroscience] Motivation-dependent communication between cortex and brainstem
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience

Neurons in the medullary brainstem exhibit movement-related patterns of activity, but the neuronal population codes that specify distinct actions, and the mechanisms by which cortex may shape these codes as a function of motivational state, remain unclear. To explore whether coupling between cortex and medulla depends upon motivational context, we trained mice to make both pre-reward "appetitive" licks that served to trigger water availability and rapidly attenuated with satiety, and "consummatory" licks, which occur post-reward release and more slowly attenuated with satiety. Simultaneous recordings from secondary motor cortex and motor medulla revealed that medullary activity was more time-locked than cortical activity to individual licks and exhibited a phase-based population code that encoded lick direction. Correlations between cortex and medulla were stronger during appetitive licks than during consummatory licks, with causal dependency established by optogenetic intervention and supported by multi-region recurrent network models. Population codes underlying behavior shared across the central nervous system, exemplified by cortico-medullary coupling, thus may depend upon the motivational context underlying action.

item.title: [33%] [bioRxiv Neuroscience] Increased Cognitive Load Expands, Stabilizes, and Aligns Visual Representation Across the Human Brain
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience

Cognitive load refers to the mental effort required to perform a task. While previous research has extensively examined its detrimental effects on neural and behavioral performance, much less is known about how the brain actively adapts to heightened demands. Across two fMRI experiments involving visual n-back tasks, we identified several fundamental properties of this adaptive process. First, higher load enhanced and expanded visual representations beyond localized visual regions, leading to widespread visual coding. At the global scale, heightened load promoted cross-regional coordination by increasing representational alignment and strengthening information encoded in interregional functional connectivity patterns. Beyond facilitating stronger visual representation, increased load also reduced neural pattern variability, which led to more stable information coding. Finally, load was encoded independently of other task-relevant information as a separate brain state, supporting its overarching role in guiding visual processing. Together, these findings revealed that the brain adapts to heightened cognitive demands by globally reorganizing neural processing to support flexible cognition.

item.title: [32%] [arXiv AI] HiMEM: Hippocampus-Inspired Memory Consolidation, Pruning, and Composition for Vision-Language-Action Models in 3D Scenes
item.description:

arXiv:2611.09355v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Memory plays a crucial role in long-horizon task execution and cross-task generalization for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models operating in complex 3D scenes. However, existing VLA memory mechanisms suffer from memory noise, particularly in complex 3D scenes, as stored episodic memories contain extensive redundant details about scene layouts, object configurations, and robot-specific states, which obscure generalizable manipulation principles and hinder cross-task transfer. To address this challenge, we first introduce a hippocampus-inspired memory consolidation mechanism that synthesizes extensive episodic experiences into a compact set of essential semantic memories, enabling VLA models to derive generalizable principles from practical experience. Second, we propose an episodic memory pruning mechanism that removes redundant episodic memories whose contents are captured by consolidated semantic memories, thereby increasing effective memory capacity and improving long-horizon task execution. Finally, to handle complex task scenarios, we develop a flexible memory composition mechanism that jointly leverages multiple episodic and semantic memories to enhance cross-scenario generalization. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus demonstrate the effectiveness of HiMEM across different VLA backbones, improving the average success rate of pi_0 from 91.88% to 98.20% on LIBERO.

item.description:

arXiv:2511.20798v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Foundation models trained on text and images have been shown to develop abstract internal features that align with human concepts and that can be directly manipulated via activation steering to alter model behaviour. These results provide early evidence that scientific foundation models can learn general representations of physical principles, and further support for the Linear Representation Hypothesis.

item.title: [30%] [arXiv AI] Subliminal Learning in Vision-Language Models
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv AI

arXiv:2611.08538v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Subliminal learning is a phenomenon in large language models (LLMs) where a teacher passes a hidden preference to a student through training data unrelated to that preference. We study whether subliminal learning also occurs in vision-language models (VLMs). Both teachers generate numbers for an unrelated visual task involving geometric shapes. Two students initialized from the same base VLM are finetuned on the same images, using numbers generated by either the biased or control teacher. Across VLMs ranging from 2B to 7B parameters, we find that both animal and facial preferences can transfer through this unrelated task. Students trained on biased-teacher outputs select the target more often than control students, with a difference of up to $\sim$10 percentage points in the animal preference task. Transfer can become stronger with more training data and varies with the target preference, model, and how the numbers are generated. Beyond preferences, we show that the biased student's explanations use more of the same words and phrases as the biased teacher's explanations than those of the control student, even when all three models select the same image. These results matter for training VLMs and show that training on unrelated data may change both a VLM's image preferences and how it explains its choices, and that transfer can become stronger with more training samples.

item.title: [30%] [arXiv Neurons and Cognition] Decoding spatial and semantic information from large-scale visual cortical activity for natural-movie reconstruction
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition

arXiv:2611.08887v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reconstructing natural visual experience from cortical population activity is a central challenge in neural decoding, particularly for calcium imaging, where signals are noisy, temporally filtered, and paired neural-video data are limited. Here we present Ca2REAL (Calcium Activity to Reconstruct Events, Appearance, and Layout), a neural-to-video framework that conditions a pretrained video diffusion model through separate layout and semantic controls derived from calcium activity. Using measured responses from 7,863 V1 neurons in one mouse, Ca2REAL reconstructed held-out natural-movie clips with 81.4% all-pairs stimulus-identification accuracy, with its clearest gains over deterministic baselines in perceptual and semantic measures. We further evaluated the framework in a stimulus-aligned virtual population of 116,705 neurons assembled from encoding-model-predicted responses across 11 independently recorded datasets. Perturbation and ablation analyses showed that reconstruction depends on distributed, stimulus-specific population structure, with layout and semantic pathways providing complementary spatial and identity information. Temporal analyses further showed improved preservation of semantic dynamics across reconstructed clips. These results show that large-scale cortical population activity constrains the spatial, semantic, and temporal structure of natural visual experience, providing a generative framework for high-fidelity neural reconstruction of dynamic visual scenes.

item.title: [30%] [arXiv AI] Programs-of-Layers in LLMs through the Lens of Cortical Areas
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv AI

arXiv:2609.31360v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inference in LLMs is conventionally a fixed-depth, fixed-order forward pass through every layer, regardless of how difficult the input is. The human brain does not work this way. Using the thalamus as a central hub, it routes information flexibly to all regions of the cortex according to demand. Li et al. (2026) recently showed, with program-of-layers (PoLar), that transformers can be given an analogous flexibility if their layers are treated as a library of functions rather than a fixed sequence. Performance improves over the standard forward pass when each input is dynamically routed through an adaptive sequence of skipped or repeated contiguous layer blocks. Reconstructing PoLar's diagnostic Monte Carlo Tree Search in more detail across 6 models, we reproduce several of its findings: skipping outperforms the standard pass, repeating outperforms skipping, and combining both outperforms either alone. Shorter programs suffice for easier questions, while harder questions require more layer repeats. For their main claim, the learned router's gain, we find what drives it. Under their setup, the router gains by repairing the format of the model's answers, which a single fixed program, selected on validation questions, does better. In our setup, with a prompt that already fixes the format, a larger data split and our search, its top prediction collapses to the standard pass on every model, although its top-5 programs together still gain. Beyond reproduction, we find in our setup that a small fixed menu of programs solves far more questions than the standard pass, and that programs which correct errors are brittle: undoing a single edit typically breaks the correction. PoLar mirrors principles of thalamo-cortical coordination between cortical-area-like transformer layers, although a working thalamus analogue, a router that picks a better program per input, remains to be found.

item.title: [30%] [arXiv AI] Characterize Then Distill: Mechanistic Reasoning in Large Output Spaces
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv AI

arXiv:2606.06840v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reasoning-trained language models can select, zero-shot, a small set of relevant labels from thousands to hundreds of thousands of candidates. We ask how they do it mechanistically, and whether the mechanism can be distilled. We treat each decision as a token-level event scored by the model's own margin: the token that picks a coarse region of the label space, the tokens that pick a label within it, and the token where the output departs from a near-miss named earlier. Attribution, exact mean-ablation, knock-in and a null calibration give individual attention heads causal standing. On clinical coding of MIMIC-IV discharge summaries, with all 5,651 candidate codes in context, a small, global, phase-structured set of heads is necessary and sufficient on essentially every summary; distinct head families read the candidate region and the earlier near-miss, and blocking what they read removes their effect; for mentions elicitable in the reasoning, a disjoint mid-layer set makes the region elicitable several tokens before the code. The structure recurs in a second reasoner. We introduce MISTILL, which, unlike chain-of-thought distillation, also supervises the student's pooled attention at these decision events. Read on heads found after training, it nearly doubles the causal recovery of the contrastive decision in a cross-family student and adds a small, seed-stable gain in one that already carries most of it, with no detected task difference at matched precision; under matched selection it exceeds a frozen random-head pool on both recovery and task score. On two corpora with human-annotated evidence (one read zero-shot, one in domain), a MISTILL student's decision heads attend to each code's evidence more, and more specifically, than a chain-of-thought-distilled student's. A pre-registered evidence-flip test detected no improvement in evidence-dependent decisions through the tested routes.

item.title: [30%] [arXiv AI] Did I See It or Think It? Probing Reality Monitoring in Vision-Language Models with Concept Injection
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv AI

arXiv:2611.09014v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent work tests whether language models can introspect by injecting a concept direction into their activations and asking whether they notice it and can name it. These studies are text-only. Vision-language models (VLMs) face an additional problem, known in cognitive psychology as reality monitoring: they must keep internally generated content separate from what they actually see. We therefore ask: can VLMs distinguish injected concepts from image content? We introduce a paradigm that varies the image and the injected concept independently. On each trial, the model reports what it sees, whether a thought was injected, and what that thought is. This design scores both whether the model identifies the concept and which source it assigns to it. Across six VLMs, only Gemma-3-27B reliably identifies injected concepts (35% vs. 3% for steering alone), with almost no false alarms. Even then, the source it reports is fragile. Strong or visual-pathway injections are reported as seen, and a visible object nearly eliminates correct thought reports. The same failure appears in ordinary captioning, where injected objects appear in up to 87% of captions of real photographs. Evaluating multimodal self-reports therefore requires checking both their content and their reported source.

item.title: [30%] [arXiv Neurons and Cognition] Structure is in the zoom: probing neural symmetry through dimensionality scaling
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition

arXiv:2611.08506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much of a neural population's measured dimensionality is the code, and how much is the act of measuring it? The slope of the participation ratio against subsample size is reported for cortical populations and for the layers of language models as a number that belongs to the system. It does not. One patch of eleven thousand mouse V1 neurons returns three slopes, 0.25 along random stimulus subsets, 0.31 along drift direction, 0.35 along neuron count, and only the middle one carries structure; the other two are the sampling floor. We split every exponent into that floor and a shift earned along a declared axis, and read the shift against two nulls: permuting the labels, and permuting them only among samples that share a nuisance. On V1 the direction-aligned shift clears the label null in eight of eight grating recordings, is positive in 32 of 32 animals in a second laboratory, and reads both sectors of the code's O(2) symmetry. The even sector sets how the ladder starts: it decides which order of adding classes climbs faster, predicts the opposite order in an equivariant network, and flows under coarse-graining by a closed-form factor that says what orientation columns do to mesoscale signals. The odd sector, carried by the direction-selective neurons, keeps the ladder climbing past half the classes. On language models the same split separates content inherited from the tokens from construction built with depth, on five architectures, and the second null shows that a grammaticality signal of twenty standard deviations is entirely carrier composition. With a floor and a declared axis, dimensionality scaling is an axis-resolved measurement, and where the axis follows a known symmetry it resolves the sector content of the code. The instrument, rung, trains no probe and reads any array or any Hugging Face model layer by layer (https://github.com/adilamin89/structure-in-the-zoom).

item.title: [29%] [arXiv Neurons and Cognition] Platonic Representations in the Human Brain: Unsupervised Recovery of Universal Geometry
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition

arXiv:2605.20496v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Strong Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that representational convergence in artificial neural networks can be harnessed constructively: embeddings can be translated across models through a universal latent space without paired data. We ask whether an analogous geometry can be recovered across human brains. Using fMRI data from the Natural Scenes Dataset, we propose a self-supervised encoder that learns subject-specific embeddings from brain data alone by exploiting repeated stimulus presentations. We show that these independently learned spaces can be translated across subjects using unsupervised orthogonal rotations, without paired cross-subject samples or intermediate model representations. Synchronizing pairwise rotations into a single shared latent space further improves cross-subject retrieval. These results provide evidence for a shared geometry in learned representations of human visual responses: subject-specific fMRI embeddings can be aligned across individuals within a common coordinate system.

item.title: [29%] [arXiv AI] Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNs for Flexible Working Memory
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv AI

arXiv:2611.06932v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in neural systems and has been implicated in cognitive functions such as memory and sequence processing. However, its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear. Here, we studied OPC by training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, we found that OPC emerges in the RNN spontaneously: the memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with oscillation amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablation studies identified three key elements required for OPC: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis revealed the emergence of content and time cells in the trained RNN, and they process item identity and sequence order separately. Recurrent connectivity analysis revealed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups. Inspired by these findings, we proposed a neural circuit model which reproduces OPC through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. Together, this study reveals how OPC arises from network structures and task demands, offers insights into the implementation and computational mechanisms of OPC in biological systems, and inspires us to develop computational models for human-like cognitive functions.

item.title: [27%] [arXiv AI] Taming the Centaur(s) with LAPITHS: a framework for a theoretically grounded interpretation of AI performances
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv AI

arXiv:2604.27927v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a framework called LAPITHS (Language model Analysis through Paradigm grounded Interpretations of Theses about Human likenesS) and use it to show that several major claims advanced by models such as CENTAUR, proposed as an artificial Unified Model of Cognition, are not theoretically or empirically justified. LAPITHS provides a principled reference point for counteracting the current behaviouristic tendency in AI research to interpret the human level performances of transformer based language models as evidence of human like underlying computation and, by extension, as signs of cognitive abilities. The novelty of LAPITHS lies in making explicit the arguments grounded in two quantitative assessments: (i) the Minimal Cognitive Grid, a theoretically motivated method for estimating the cognitive plausibility of artificial systems, and (ii) a behavioural comparison showing that results similar to those reported for CENTAUR like models can be reproduced by other systems that do not satisfy the structural constraints typically associated with cognitive plausibility, and whose outputs do not provide independent explanatory insight into human cognition.

item.title: [27%] [arXiv AI] Generative Latent Priors for Interpreting and Steering Protein Language Models
item.description:

arXiv:2611.09818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dominant methods for interpreting large models impose strong structural assumptions. Generative Latent Priors (GLP) are a complementary approach: a diffusion model that learns the distribution of a frozen model's activations directly, imposing no assumptions. We port GLP to ESM-2 activations (UniRef50) and evaluate it at two host scales (ESM-2-8M and -650M), both as a lens for protein representations and as a prior for editing them. Generation quality scales smoothly with depth and compute. As a lens, single GLP "meta-neurons" are the strongest probes of discrete Swiss-Prot concepts at both hosts, beating InterPLM's released SAE features, and lead on continuous properties at 8M though not at 650M; falsification tests show this is mostly concentration, not new information. As an editing prior, the on-manifold correction makes DiffMean steering of three biochemical properties effective and restores on-manifoldness, but only in isolation: re-embedding the sequences actually produced after several rounds of decoding, the structural plausibility is compromised. This is mainly reproduced in additional SAE-based clamping structural steering experiments, where only Helix motif succeeds. The naturalness failure is traced to the rewriting coverage and the decoder rather than the prior, highlighting what the method must clear before it can serve for both discovery-by-editing and discovery-by-exploration. Trained GLPs are released on huggingface.co/collections/HPAI-BSC/glprot.

item.title: [27%] [arXiv AI] AlienBench: A Benchmark of Structural Novelty in Language Model Outputs
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv AI

arXiv:2611.09094v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for creative tasks such as writing, design, and idea generation. For these uses, it matters whether a model's ideas depart from familiar examples or stay close to them. Novelty is one standard measure of creativity, and current creativity evaluations ask human experts or LLM judges to rate how novel an output is. However, these ratings have no fixed reference for what counts as novel (or, in other terms, departure from the familiar). Measuring this departure requires a task with known familiar defaults. The structured imagination task from cognitive psychology is such a task. In this creativity test, people imagine a creature from another planet. The departure from features of Earth animals, such as bilateral symmetry and legs as mode of locomotion, is used as measure of creativity. We introduce AlienBench, a benchmark that adapts the structured imagination task to language models. Models describe alien creatures, and a panel of three LLM judges extracts ten biological features from the description and labels them as either Earth-typical or a departure. The sum of feature departures is the score of a description, from 0 to 10. Each model describes alien creatures under six prompt conditions that vary the framing of the task and the planetary environment. Each model generates 30 descriptions per condition (180 in total), and its overall score is the mean across these descriptions. We evaluate 10 language models, from frontier to open-weight models. Overall scores range from 3.28 (GPT-6 Luna) to 6.55 (Ministral 3 14B). Interestingly, open-weight models score higher than proprietary models in this task (5.40 vs. 4.58). Under the baseline prompt, the models depart from Earth defaults more often on average than 100 human participants on every feature. We release all prompts, generations, judge outputs, and scores.

item.title: [27%] [arXiv AI] AtariBench: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in Atari Gameplay
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv AI

arXiv:2611.08755v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on static visual understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to act in dynamic environments remains less well understood. We introduce AtariBench, a controlled benchmark that evaluates VLMs across 20 Atari 2600 games, requiring models to make sequential decisions from high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams. By decoupling fast in-game dynamics from wall-clock inference speed, AtariBench focuses on whether models can perceive rapid visual state changes, reason over spatiotemporal dynamics, and ground actions in the current observation. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations in state-of-the-art VLMs: models often fail to infer object motion and direction, exhibit brittle sequential decision-making, and over-rely on textual interaction history despite newly appended visual feedback. We further introduce a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores provide reliable signals of model competence, and use the benchmark to study how memory design and prompting strategies affect performance. Overall, AtariBench exposes a persistent gap between passive visual perception and active decision-making, providing a lightweight and rigorous testbed for developing VLMs that can reason and act in dynamic environments.

item.title: [27%] [arXiv AI] A Stochastic Latent Variable Generalization of Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv AI

arXiv:2611.09302v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) predict the latent embedding of a target signal from a context signal, with an auxiliary variable z conditioning the predictor. Despite its prominent role in the original JEPA blueprint, the content of z has been carried by a fixed deterministic token in every prior instantiation, collapsing the genuinely multi-modal distribution over plausible completions to a point estimate. We present S-JEPA, which realises z as a proper stochastic latent variable for masked image prediction: a learned posterior infers z from context and target during training, while a learned context-conditioned prior approximates the distribution of plausible completions at inference, with no decoders and no reconstruction. In its deterministic limit the objective reduces to the I-JEPA loss in functional form, generalising that objective rather than strictly containing the I-JEPA model. Our central finding is that stochasticity adds capabilities, error-correlated predictive uncertainty and diverse completions, at no cost to representation quality: under matched architectures and schedules S-JEPA improves over the deterministic I-JEPA baseline and exceeds LeJEPA at matched architecture, while additionally producing spatially structured uncertainty maps and semantically diverse completions, neither of which the deterministic predictor produces.

item.title: [27%] [arXiv AI] BabyTheorist: A Benchmark for Learning to Theorize the World from Observation Alone
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv AI

arXiv:2611.08177v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How would we know whether a machine truly understands the world? We argue that one key capability is observational theory learning: acquiring reusable theories from pure observations and applying them to new situations. Current visual reasoning benchmarks focus primarily on the latter, presenting each task as a few-shot puzzle grouped by a common rule. We introduce BabyTheorist, a benchmark for controlled training and evaluation of observational theory learning. BabyTheorist generates continual streams of before-after visual observations from hidden compositional programs; during training, learners see only the resulting transitions, with no program labels, task identities, or support sets. To support theory learning and evaluation, BabyTheorist controls the program language, a curriculum over program complexity, recurring frequent subprograms, and a continual train-test protocol with level skipping. Seven representative baselines plateau well below ceiling, with the gap widening as the curriculum advances---evidence that BabyTheorist isolates a capability current program-learning approaches do not yet address.

item.title: [26%] [bioRxiv Neuroscience] Confidence: Its Measurement, Relation to Behavior, and Neural Representation
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience

Confidence (certainty/uncertainty about one's own decision) has attracted considerable attention in psychology, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence. Yet its relation to behavior remains unclear: Some treat confidence as a cause of behavior whereas others view it as a state controlled by environmental variables. The unobservable nature of confidence makes its measurement validation and analyses difficult. To tackle these issues, we developed a novel procedure combining a decision-making task, risk choices, and a post-task open-ended questionnaire. Point-gain/loss amounts for correct/incorrect decisions varied depending on choices between high-risk/high-return and low-risk/low-return. In the questionnaire, 90% of 16 participants reported feelings interpretable as certainty/uncertainty when making those risk choices despite no instruction about confidence, whereas 8% did so when the choices led to identical outcomes/returns. This suggests confidence is a state controlled by environmental contingencies rather than a cause of behavior. We also decoded changes in the state from electroencephalography and functional magnetic resonance imaging.

item.title: [26%] [bioRxiv Neuroscience] Probing EEG Foundation Model Attention Maps for Lightweight Interpretable Emotion Recognition
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience

Foundation Models (FMs) trained on EEG signals promise subject- and dataset-independent pipelines for brain-computer interface (BCI) applications, but have yet to consistently outperform task-specific architectures, and their large representations are costly to compute and store. As a means of advancing the understanding of the Foundation Models' inner mechanisms, we propose a lightweight alternative that exploits the self-attention mechanism of REVE, a pretrained EEG FM, to derive features similar to weighted Functional Connectivity (FC) without any fine-tuning. Inspired by kernel-based FC matrices, we aggregate the raw first-layer attention weights of a single head over the full duration of dataset trials into weighted channel-to-channel adjacency matrices. These matrices replace standard encoder representation vectors as classification features, substantially reducing computational cost. We further introduce a label-free, symmetry-based criterion, motivated by the emergence of near-symmetric attention patterns in trained encoder-decoder transformers, ranking attention heads by how much discriminative information they carry. Classical machine learning classifiers are then trained on the single most informative head's attention-derived FC matrix and achieve balanced accuracy and F1 scores on the SEED-IV emotion-recognition dataset that are competitive with several fully fine-tuned state-of-the-art EEG Foundation Models, requiring at least two orders of magnitude fewer calculations than the standard use of the encoder. Subsequent cortical region analysis revealed a significant over-representation of frontal region connections by ranking the most discriminative FC matrix connectivity edges, validating our methods as consistent with prior affective-computing literature. These results suggest that interpretable, computationally inexpensive linear probing of attention maps is a viable route to deploying EEG Foundation Models in resource-constrained settings.

item.title: [100%] [eLife Neuroscience] The resource elasticity of control
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: eLife Neuroscience

The ability to determine how much the environment can be controlled through our actions has long been viewed as fundamental to adaptive behavior. While traditional accounts treat controllability as a fixed property of the environment, we argue that real-world controllability often depends on the effort, time, and money we are able and willing to invest. In such cases, controllability can be said to be elastic to invested resources. Here, we propose that inferring this elasticity is essential for efficient resource allocation, and thus, elasticity misestimations result in maladaptive behavior. To test this hypothesis, we developed a novel treasure hunt game where participants encountered environments with varying degrees of controllability and elasticity. Across two pre-registered studies ( N =514), we first demonstrate that people infer elasticity and adapt their resource allocation accordingly. We then present a computational model that explains how people make this inference and identify individual elasticity biases that lead to suboptimal resource allocation. Finally, we show that overestimation of elasticity is associated with elevated psychopathology involving an impaired sense of control. These findings establish the elasticity of control as a distinct cognitive construct guiding adaptive behavior and a computational marker for control-related maladaptive behavior.

item.title: [100%] [eLife Neuroscience] The hypoxic response extends lifespan through a bioaminergic and peptidergic neural circuit
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: eLife Neuroscience

A coordinated response to stress is crucial for promoting the short- and long-term health of an organism. The perception of stress, frequently through the nervous system, can lead to physiological changes that are fundamental to maintaining homeostasis. Activating the response to low oxygen, or hypoxia, extends healthspan and lifespan in Caenorhabditis elegans . However, despite some positive impacts, negative effects of the hypoxic response in specific tissues prevent translation of their benefits in mammals. Thus, it is imperative to identify which components of this response promote longevity. Here, we interrogate the cell-nonautonomous signaling pathway downstream of genetic activation of the hypoxic response. We find that HIF-1-mediated signaling in ADF serotonergic neurons is both necessary and sufficient for lifespan extension. Signaling through the serotonin receptor SER-7 in the GABAergic RIS interneurons is necessary in this process. Our findings also highlight the involvement of additional neural signaling molecules, including the neurotransmitters tyramine and GABA, and the neuropeptide NLP-17, in mediating longevity effects. Finally, we demonstrate that oxygen- and carbon-dioxide-sensing neurons act downstream of HIF-1 in this circuit. Together, these insights demonstrate a circuit for how genetic induction of the hypoxic response cell-nonautonomously modifies aging and suggests valuable targets for modulating aging in mammals.

item.title: [100%] [eLife Neuroscience] Simple methods to acutely measure multiple timing metrics among the sexual repertoire of male Drosophila
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: eLife Neuroscience

Male Drosophila courtship behavior is a key model for studying temporal decision-making. While courtship index (CI) is widely used to quantify mating activity, other timing metrics like courtship latency, copulation latency (CL), and mating duration (MD) remain understudied. Traditional methods for quantifying these behaviors are often labor-intensive and prone to human error. In this study, we present a protocol combining a modular chamber system and automated software (DrosoMating) to quantify six key timing metrics during male courtship. Our image-based video analysis enables precise identification of courtship and copulation events, as well as quantification of their timing and duration under controlled conditions. Validation shows <0.05% error rates and 98–99% agreement with manual scoring for CL, CI, and MD. The protocol supports genetic and neural circuit manipulations, detecting subtle genetic, social, and environmental behavioral variations. By minimizing manual effort and standardizing data collection, this approach facilitates scalable, reproducible studies on adaptive trade-offs, learning, and neural mechanisms in mating behavior. This method streamlines timing analysis in male courtship, offering reproducible metrics for behavioral genetics.

item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: eLife Neuroscience

The visual system can flexibly adjust attentional deployment to match task demands, but whether observers can proactively modulate the spatial scope of attention based on expectations about upcoming search difficulty remains unclear. According to the zoom lens model, attention can narrow or broaden its spatial extent, with narrower focus enhancing processing efficiency, a mechanism that would benefit target discrimination in crowded displays. We tested whether observers adjust attentional scope when expecting sparse versus dense search arrays by combining spatial cueing with block-wise manipulations of display density expectations. Participants performed a visual search task in which endogenous cues predicted target location, while blocks predominantly contained either sparse (1 target, 3 distractors) or dense (1 target, 7 distractors) displays. We applied inverted encoding models to broadband EEG data to reconstruct spatial channel tuning functions, enabling precise characterization of both the locus and breadth of attentional deployment. Behaviorally, expecting difficult searches selectively improved accuracy at cued locations without costs elsewhere. Consistent with this selective benefit, neural measurements revealed that expectancy enhanced the amplitude of spatially selective responses at the attended location but did not alter tuning width. These findings demonstrate that expectations about search difficulty modulate attention through gain-based signal enhancement rather than adjustments to spatial scope, revealing that preparatory attentional control operates via amplitude modulation within a stable spatial focus. This mechanism complements reactive attentional adjustments and provides an efficient means for the visual system to optimize processing under predictable task demands.

item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: eLife Neuroscience

Heartbeat and behavior are tightly coordinated during defensive states, yet the neuronal mechanisms linking threat processing to cardiac modulation—and the potential contribution of cardiac dynamics to behavioral output—remain poorly understood. Here, using simultaneous recordings of heartbeat and behavior in tethered Drosophila , we show that mechanical threat triggers locomotion together with rapid cardiac deceleration. We identify two pairs of dopaminergic neurons, termed DA-WED neurons, that mediate this cardiac response. Silencing these neurons markedly attenuates threat-induced cardiac deceleration, whereas optogenetic activation induces cardiac deceleration in the absence of threat. Two-photon calcium imaging further shows that DA-WED neurons are activated by mechanical threat, and manipulating their activity bidirectionally modulates threat-induced locomotion. Linking cardiac dynamics to behavior, direct optogenetic manipulation of cardiomyocytes that quantitatively reproduces threat-evoked cardiac deceleration is accompanied by increased locomotion. Together, these results identify a dopaminergic descending pathway that links threat processing to cardiac modulation and suggest that cardiac dynamics may contribute to shaping defensive behavior.

item.title: [100%] [eLife Neuroscience] Distinct neural representations of perceptual and numerical absence in the human brain
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: eLife Neuroscience

The ability to represent absences is fundamental to human perception and cognition. Sensitivity to non-numerical absences depends on inferring a lack of sensory evidence, enabling the recognition of a lack of environmental resources or other objects. In turn, encoding numerical absence as a concept – in the form of the number zero – has enabled a multitude of technological and mathematical advances. Whether perceptual and conceptual absences rely on overlapping or distinct neural representations in the human brain, however, remains unknown. We employed three different tasks together with magnetoencephalography to characterise neural representations of absence evoked within perceptual and numerical domains. Using multivariate decoding and Bayes factor analyses, we replicate previous findings of shared representations of numerical absence across symbolic and non-symbolic formats. In contrast, we show that these representations of numerical absence are distinct from those evoked by non-numerical absences. This result held even after controlling for stimulus-level confounds which generate surface-level similarities between perceptual absences and non-symbolic empty sets. Our results extend a boundary between perception and cognition to the domain of absence and provide insight into the different mechanisms employed by the human brain to both perceive and conceive of absences.

item.title: [100%] [eLife Neuroscience] Spectraplakin is required for dendritic microtubule organization via a tip-based mechanism in Drosophila
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: eLife Neuroscience

The differential microtubule organization in axons and dendrites underlies neuronal polarity and developmental processes, like neurite pruning. How neurons achieve their specific microtubule organization during development is an area of active research, and it has been especially hard to explain how dendritic microtubules are oriented with their plus ends toward the soma. Transient microtubule nucleation from tips of early growing dendrites has been proposed as a mechanism that would explain how this orientation is set up. In a survey for cytoskeletal regulators involved in dendrite pruning and microtubule organization in Drosophila , we found the spectraplakin Short stop (Shot), an actin/microtubule crosslinker. Loss of Shot causes microtubule orientation defects already during early dendrite development, when Shot is transiently recruited to tips of growing dendrites via its actin-binding domain. Genetic and functional evidence suggests that Shot’s primary function in this process is to locally stabilize microtubules. We also provide evidence for an independent, developmentally transient microtubule nucleation mechanism. Our data highlight the importance of transient and localized microtubule regulation for dendritic microtubule organization.

item.title: [100%] [eLife Neuroscience] A validated antibody toolbox for ALS research
item.description:

A substantial fraction of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-associated proteins remains poorly characterized, in part because of the limited availability of validated research antibodies. We established knockout (KO)-based antibody characterization workflows and demonstrated that widely used antibodies against the major ALS-associated protein C9orf72 lacked specificity (Laflamme et al., 2019). Here, we extend this approach by establishing the ALS-Reproducible Antibody Platform (ALS-RAP), a comprehensive effort to generate a publicly available dataset of KO-validated antibodies targeting proteins encoded by ALS risk genes. In total, we characterized 303 antibodies against 33 ALS-associated proteins to identify high-quality reagents for use in western blot, immunoprecipitation, and immunofluorescence. Using these antibodies, we profiled protein levels across human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived and primary neurological cell types. These analyses revealed diverse cellular distributions and higher levels of several ALS-associated proteins in glial populations, consistent with emerging evidence for immune contributions to ALS. Together, ALS-RAP provides a validated antibody toolbox and protein expression resource to support the study of ALS-associated proteins.

item.title: [100%] [eLife Neuroscience] Spyglass is a framework for reproducible and shareable neuroscience research
item.description:

Scientific progress depends on reliable and reproducible results. Progress can be accelerated when data are shared and re-analyzed to address new questions. Current approaches to storing and analyzing neural data involve bespoke formats and software that make replication and reuse of data difficult. To address these challenges, we created Spyglass, an open-source data management and analysis framework written in Python. Spyglass provides reproducible pipelines for common neuroscience analyses and sharing of raw data, intermediate analyses, and final results within and across labs. Spyglass uses the Neurodata Without Borders (NWB) standard and includes pipelines for spectral filtering, spike sorting, pose tracking, and neural decoding. Spyglass can be extended to apply existing and newly developed pipelines to datasets from multiple sources. item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Trends at 50: a mission that matters
item.description:

What makes a great review article in your field? As more research is published every day, it has become increasingly difficult to keep up with the latest developments and to ensure that you are hearing from the leading scientists driving these innovations and advances. How do you know what is new and what is valuable?

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] A new view of collectivism
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

Collectivism is the most widely studied cultural dimension. Yet recent evidence shows that the most-cited scales contain conflicting definitions of collectivism. I review evidence that conceptualizations conflate ‘warm fuzzy’ collectivism and responsibilism. I outline how clarifying the concept can resolve apparent contradictions in previous findings and advance measurement and theory.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Consumer neuroscience: the emerging science of everyday choices
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

Consumer neuroscience is a developing field at the intersection of neuroscience, psychology, economics, and marketing that seeks to uncover the neural and physiological mechanisms underlying consumer behavior. Building on early psychophysiological studies, the field has expanded substantially since the mid-2000s through an increasing range of methods and models. We highlight that its strength lies in spanning multiple levels of analysis to address marketing-relevant questions. We highlight four major trends driving the field: improving behavioral prediction, synthesizing evidence through multidataset analyses, developing formal models linking neural processes to consumer decision-making, and integrating brain and body measures. Together, these advances position consumer neuroscience as an integrative science with implications for marketing, policy, and consumer welfare.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] A consonant bias in dogs
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

Do dogs perceive speech similarly to humans? A recent work by Morvai et al. suggests that dogs develop a focus on consonants to identify words, resembling results observed in humans. This is likely the result of massive exposure to language combined with an evolutionarily ancient ability to track regularities in the signal.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Lost, then found: transient forgetting in humans and machines
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

Forgetting can be permanent or transient. An intriguing, recently described form of transient forgetting (TF) in artificial neural networks is the stability gap: a network that has already learned a first task exhibits transient yet substantial forgetting when it begins additional training on a second task alongside the first. Could an analogous phenomenon be found in humans? Following a literature survey, six types of TF in humans were identified, categorised by their sources: learning, retrieval, spontaneous, overgeneralisation, task-switching, and multitasking. Although all differ in important ways from the stability gap, it is hypothesised that some underlying mechanisms are shared. This opinion article concludes by proposing experiments to test whether a ‘stability gap-like’ form of TF also occurs in humans.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] What can behavior tell us about neural dynamics?
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

For decades, systems neuroscience treated behavior as an endpoint: a simplified output, such as a button press, lick, or saccade, used to isolate neural computations. Richer behavioral measurements have expanded this view by revealing neural dynamics hidden by simple outputs. Yet behavior is not a direct readout of brain activity, because similar behavioral outputs can arise from different neural mechanisms. Interpreting neural dynamics is therefore an inverse problem with no straightforward solution. Behavior can constrain this problem by exposing sensorimotor loops, narrowing plausible explanations for population activity, and formalizing neural–behavioral relationships in joint models. Together, these approaches position behavior as a principled constraint on interpreting neural dynamics and latent cognitive, affective, and computational states.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Peripersonal space: a neural system mapping self–environment interaction ‘here and now’
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

The space surrounding the body where physical interactions with external stimuli occur is referred to as peripersonal space (PPS). Traditionally conceived as a spatial construct, PPS is better understood as a neural representation that integrates bodily inputs with external cues to predict body–object interactions. After summarizing its multisensory, motor, and plastic properties, this review draws on computational models to examine how PPS captures statistical regularities of body–object interactions. This predictive function may position PPS as an interface between self and environment, contributing to minimal self-consciousness and its alterations across states of consciousness and neuropsychiatric conditions. Recent findings extend this framework to the inner body, suggesting that interoceptive signals shape PPS and that PPS-related processing may influence immune responses.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Mate preferences and the compatibility puzzle
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

Researchers and laypeople commonly assume that romantic attraction depends, at least in part, on whether potential partners possess the traits that a person says they want. Yet recent studies suggest that such preference-matching effects (Preference × Trait statistical interactions) are often surprisingly small or even absent. Possible psychological explanations include (i) mate choice is multivariate, and so the matching effect for any given trait is heavily constrained, and (ii) traits permit flexible interpretations, in that the same trait can be interpreted differently depending on the partner to whom the trait belongs. Compatibility may derive not mainly from the matching of preferences and traits but rather from the way that two people recurrently extend and build upon shared positive experiences over time.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] What can machine learning discover about the nature of emotion?
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

The science of emotion increasingly relies on machine learning (ML) in the hope of making objective discoveries that resolve century-long debates. We examine research strategies in two main research traditions and show how confirmation bias can arise when theory-based hypotheses are evaluated using theory-laden sampling strategies, model specifications, and inferences. Each tradition manifests its theoretical differences in its ML methods, and, therefore, ML methods cannot settle those differences. The reciprocal relationships between starting assumptions, findings, and conclusions illustrate that ML investigations of emotion, like all scientific investigations, are never free from human experience and beliefs; however, they can be made less biased through a theory-aware research strategy to generate more justified knowledge about emotion.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Dependency grammar remains the simplest theory of grammar: a reply to Fujita
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

In the original article [1], I claimed that dependency grammar is the simplest theory of grammar. All theories of grammar have rules for connecting words together to make larger units. In dependency grammar, these connections are directly between words. In phrase structure grammars, there is slightly more structure than in dependency grammar, consisting of nonterminal categories for the connected elements, such as the noun phrase and the verb phrase. I argued that these two alternatives are somewhat interchangeable.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Evidence supports constituency-based syntax, movement, and unpronounced elements
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

Gibson advocates dependency grammar [1], contrasting it with constituency-based accounts that posit movement and phonologically null (unpronounced) syntactic elements [2,3]. Dependency grammar represents sentence structure through word-to-word relations, whereas constituency-based accounts represent sentence structure by grouping words into larger hierarchical constituents. Movement accounts for cases in which a constituent appears in one position but is interpreted in another. For example, in ‘Who did you call?’, ‘Who’ appears sentence-initially but is interpreted as the object of ‘call’; this is analysed as movement from the object position to the sentence-initial position.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Selection-for-prediction: rethinking early cognitive development
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

For decades, core knowledge accounts have proposed that early cognition is organized by innate, domain-specific conceptual or concept-like representations of objects, physical events, number, and agents. I propose a different starting point: infants’ behaviors may arise from domain-general attentional priors—evolutionarily shaped selection biases—interacting with perceptual mechanisms that organize information and support perceptual prediction, rather than from abstract, postperceptual representations. Attentional priors favor ecologically consequential information, including continuity, contact, and synchrony. When such information is disrupted, perceptual prediction error—rather than conceptual contradiction—may produce violation-of-expectation effects. Grounded in constraints on visual input and neural processing, this framework accounts for early successes and systematic failures, suggesting that development begins with perceptual-attentional mechanisms that shape selection, organization, prediction, and learning.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Sound asleep, yet still listening: auditory processing during human sleep
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

Sleepers can wake to their name, but ignore louder irrelevant sounds, a paradox that suggests more than simple sensory gating. Growing evidence reveals flexible auditory coupling during human sleep, ranging from complete disconnection to high-level cognitive processing and even to physical responses. Here, we synthesize the multiple cognitive levels at which auditory stimuli are processed (or not) during human sleep and outline factors modulating this processing. Moments of sensory isolation may promote restoration and memory consolidation, while moments of environmental coupling enable threat detection. We speculate that no single optimal balance exists; rather, the ideal degree of sensory coupling shifts with individuals and contexts. Chronic dysregulation of this balance may contribute to the clinical picture of sleep disorders, including insomnia and hypersomnia.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Beyond accuracy: interoceptive self-appraisal and the meaning of bodily signals
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

For decades, accuracy in detecting internal bodily signals has been considered an important component of emotional experience. Yet this link remains elusive. Across methods and domains, interoceptive accuracy shows inconsistent associations with emotion and psychopathology. We argue this mismatch reflects a hierarchy of interoceptive processing: accuracy measures capture how bodily signals are detected, whereas emotion depends on metacognitive appraisals of what those signals mean, their reliability, and what they imply about the self. We introduce interoceptive self-appraisal (ISA) as a higher-order process through which bodily sensations are interpreted in context and assigned significance. ISA provides a framework for investigating affective vulnerability and developmental pathways to psychopathology. By integrating disparate theories of bodily appraisal, we outline a roadmap for interoception research.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Time after time: neural codes of speech comprehension
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

The acoustic signal of speech is fleeting and unfolds linearly; yet listeners must derive temporally extended and hierarchically organized linguistic structures to comprehend it. This article reviews evidence that the human brain transforms the transient auditory signal into neural representations that are persistent, parallel, and time-stamped. First, neural persistence allows information to remain available after it has disappeared from the acoustic input. Second, parallel encoding of recent inputs across multiple levels of language structure enables composition and interactions across the speech hierarchy. Third, dynamic neural representations encode both content and elapsed time, providing a flexible mechanism for preserving sequence order. Together, these representational properties reveal how the human brain transforms a continuously disappearing signal into temporally extended linguistic structures.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Childhood maltreatment and the developing brain: toward individualized models of psychiatric risk
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

Childhood maltreatment shapes brain development in ways that vary by adversity type, developmental timing, and genetic vulnerability to psychiatric illness—a heterogeneity that conventional approaches capture poorly. We contend that normative modeling, multivariate methods, and polygenic risk scores offer complementary frameworks for parsing this variability and advancing mechanistic insights and clinical stratification.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] The next generation of fear generalization
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

Generalizing from past experience is a fundamental feature of cognition. Although generalization has been of long-standing interest to diverse domains in psychological science, the past decade has seen a rapid acceleration of fear generalization research in particular. The field of human fear generalization is at a pivotal juncture where it is now possible to synthesize extensive behavioral work, competing theoretical models, animal and human neuroscience, and clinical and individual-differences research to address enduring gaps. In this review, we provide an updated account of where the field of human fear generalization currently resides and offer concrete avenues for new research emphasizing tighter integration between animal and human neuroscience, prioritizing cross-disciplinary perspectives, and updating conceptual frameworks to align with rapidly advancing methods.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Valuation as a bridge between aesthetics and creativity
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

Evidence shows that aesthetic evaluations are underpinned by mechanisms in the reward system that compute value for objects of interest. In turn, recent behavioral, computational, and neuroimaging evidence suggests that creativity involves a similar valuation process, as people generate and evaluate the originality and adequacy of their ideas—two standard criteria of creativity. item.description:

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Wired for coherence: a network theory of self
item.description:

item.description:

item.description:

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Rethinking reciprocity
item.description:

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Misinformation as strategy: Epistemic consequences and the undermining of shared truth
item.description:

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Geographical psychology: Spatial variation in psychological phenomena and their consequences
item.description:

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Searching beyond decrements: Attentional guidance across the adult lifespan
item.description:

item.description:

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Timescapes of non-human experience
item.description:

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Building word meanings from memories and predictions
item.description:

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] To model human linguistic prediction, make LLMs less superhuman
item.description:

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Online planning of sequential actions
item.description:

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Cognitive computations underlying ritual performance and persistence
item.description:

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Embracing the suboptimal organization of the human brain
item.description:

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Openness to Experience: from ecology to culture
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Cognitive Sciences

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Attention in the wild: balancing flexibility and stability
item.description:

item.description:

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Cognitive Sciences] Dependency syntax as the simplest theory of grammar

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Neurosciences] Constructing events across perception, action, and thought
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Neurosciences

The brain organizes continuous experience into events that structure episodic memory and guide behavior. Traditional accounts have primarily focused on sensory discontinuities and prediction errors that trigger updates of event models. Here, we broaden this view to consider event boundaries arising during goal-directed behavior, spontaneous thought, and memory recall, including transitions generated in the absence of corresponding changes in sensory input. We propose that prediction error and uncertainty provide complementary signals for event model updating: prediction errors signal a violation of current expectations, whereas uncertainty may promote updating when upcoming states become difficult to predict. We further suggest that the hippocampus may serve as a candidate hub linking boundary-related representational changes across perception, action, and thought. Together, this framework offers an integrative account of how the brain detects and generates event structure in continuous experience to support memory and behavior.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Neurosciences] Evolving perspectives on cardiac innervation: from relay to a complex regulated network
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Neurosciences

Neural control of the heart adjusts cardiac output to the functional demands of the body in order to maintain homeostasis. Sensory afferents monitor blood pressure, metabolites, and other parameters, sending information to the brainstem that then alters the balance of stimulatory sympathetic and inhibitory parasympathetic transmission to the heart. ‘Autonomic imbalance’ between sympathetic and parasympathetic efferent transmission in the heart is a characteristic of cardiovascular and metabolic diseases that contributes to pathology. In this review, we discuss recent studies related to the peripheral components of the cardiac control circuit. We summarize data from induced pluripotent stem cells, small and large animal models, and human studies that reveal more complexity in peripheral components of this system than previously understood. We also discuss peripheral neuroplasticity in cardiovascular disease and the potential impact of neuromodulation therapies.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Neurosciences] Organization of neuropeptide signaling: cross-species insights from small model organisms
item.description:
Relevance: 100% | Source: Trends in Neurosciences

Neuropeptides are ancient signaling molecules that modulate neural circuit function and behavior across the animal kingdom. Model organisms such as Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogaster, and zebrafish serve as powerful in vivo models for deciphering the organization of neuropeptidergic signaling, owing to their smaller nervous systems, genetic tractability, and the growing availability of neural connectomes. In this article, we review how these organisms have advanced current understanding of neuropeptidergic transmission across three interconnected themes: (i) the roles of peptides in sensory–motor transformations, (ii) the conservation and divergence of peptidergic expression and network architecture across species, and (iii) the diversity of neurotransmission strategies employed by single neurons. Finally, we highlight recent technological innovations as well as open questions that could shape this field in the coming years.

item.description:

These processes are driven by neurotrophic factors, axon guidance cues, extracellular vesicles, and stress-associated pathways. The functional consequences of innervation are context-dependent, with sympathetic, parasympathetic, and sensory inputs exerting distinct effects across tumor types and stages. We conclude by outlining key challenges and future directions for therapeutic translation.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Neurosciences] Apolipoprotein E4 and immune dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease: mechanisms and therapeutic implications

In the central nervous system, APOE4 pushes microglia away from homeostatic surveillance toward metabolically stressed, inflammatory, and synaptotoxic phenotypes, thereby weakening pathological protein clearance and promoting neurodegeneration. In the periphery, APOE4 primes innate and adaptive immune cells toward a pro-inflammatory state, creating a reservoir that can communicate with the diseased brain and infiltrate it. In addition, APOE4 erodes the separation between central and peripheral immune compartments, enabling bidirectional immune crosstalk that amplifies neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. In this review, we synthesize evidence for APOE4-driven central and peripheral immune dysregulation; discuss therapeutic opportunities for targeting the APOE4 immune axis; and highlight the need for human-derived, longitudinal, cross-tissue studies to identify causal, stage-specific, and targetable immune nodes for precision intervention.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Neurosciences] Resilience and vulnerability in the midbrain dopamine system during aging
item.description:

In this review, we first examine the impact of healthy aging on the dopamine system across sexes and species, including flies, mice, rats, and humans. We next consider the neuroadaptive mechanisms that sustain dopamine neuron function with age. Finally, we contrast the molecular mechanisms of age-related neurodegenerative diseases with those of healthy aging, exploring the possibility that loss of neuroadaptive reserve drives dopamine neurodegeneration. Elucidating these neuroadaptive mechanisms could offer a path toward preserving dopamine neuron function across the lifespan and potentially preventing age-related neurodegeneration.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Neurosciences] The mitochondrial epigenome and noncoding genome in aging and brain diseases

Furthermore, these mechanisms are altered in aging, neurodegenerative disease, and acute brain injury. In this review, we synthesize emerging insights into how the mitochondrial epigenome and noncoding genome shape mitochondrial function and serve as regulatory interfaces linking cellular stress and neuronal vulnerability in brain aging and disease.

item.title: [100%] [Trends in Neurosciences] Sleep-dependent microglial functions in Alzheimer’s disease
item.description:

Delineating the different functions played by microglia during specific brain states, such as sleep, represents an active area of research. In this article, we review a growing literature supporting the notion that sleep dynamically shapes microglial functional outputs. We further suggest that the failure of the sleep–microglia axis may represent an important component of the molecular framework of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), contributing to disease progression. Finally, we discuss preclinical and clinical evidence suggesting that sleep-targeting interventions may modulate AD pathology, and highlight the possibility that restoring sleep physiology could recalibrate microglial homeostatic functions and slow disease progression.

In this article, we review the current state of neural decoding advancements and their projected trajectory to assess what current and foreseeable technologies can reveal about mental states and the implications for mental privacy. Drawing on a neuroscientific perspective, we clarify the scope and limits of emerging mental privacy risks and argue for a shift in responsibility from reactive regulation to proactive, privacy-embedded design.
